country.comment: Historical case study of the municipality of Barreiro (Setúbal Peninsula) within continental Portugal; comparative secondary context on Aveiro, Lisbon, Figueira da Foz, and brief concluding comparisons with Spain and other European countries are also noted.

effect_estimate.comment: Archival historical-institutional case study with descriptive administrative and hydrogeological figures rather than statistical regression estimates (note: cell values inside embedded image Tables 1-3 are not printed in the extracted text layer, so only exact figures stated in the body text are reported).
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported. Archival records show that mandatory piped connections and compulsory minimum water charges for buildings with rents above 100 escudos (Decreto-Lei 23:707 of 1934; Decreto 29:216 of 1938) improved public sanitation in Barreiro but created affordability barriers and widespread non-payment: unpaid bills reached nearly one-quarter of issued bills in 1942, accumulated to 125% in 1943, and reached three-quarters in 1944. Raising the mandatory-payment rent threshold to 200 escudos/month (full exemption up to 200 escudos/month and tiered minimum consumption of 2 m3 for 200-400 escudos, 3 m3 for 400-800 escudos, and 5 m3 above 800 escudos) enabled new consumer contracts in lower-income brackets from 1944. Meanwhile, insufficient municipal capacity for heavy industry, state credit incentives for private groundwater works (Decreto-Lei 39:755 of 1954), and continued private industrial extraction despite a 1960 restriction on wells deeper than 50 m except for public supply (Decreto-Lei 43:371 of 1960) contributed to a 779% rise in pumped groundwater across Almada, Seixal, and Barreiro between 1961 and 1978 (with northern Setúbal piezometric levels falling 5-10 m in 1969-1978), resulting in severe aquifer overexploitation and salinization/contamination.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF pp. 7-11, Section 2 & Conclusiones

mechanism_certainty.comment: Rated 2 (mechanism directly observed/documented empirically; at the design ceiling of 2 for Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework): municipal utility annual reports (Serviços Municipalizados, 1942-1945), corporate records, and Portuguese decrees directly document how compulsory connection/minimum-tariff rules caused widespread bill non-payment among low-income residents, how the 1944 rent-threshold exemption reform enabled new low-tier contracts, and how state credit and partial well restrictions interacted with industrial self-supply to drive aquifer depletion.

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Primary historical-institutional / legal-empirical case study based on archival municipal and corporate records, parliamentary proceedings, and statutory decrees, with no human-subjects survey, interview, or quasi-experimental design; fits the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework.

sample_size.comment: Single-municipality historical archival case study of Barreiro (Setúbal); the paper does not report a numeric count of archival documents consulted or a survey/interview sample size (contextual national figures for 273 municipal seats and rural settlements in 1956 are cited on PDF p. 6, and Barreiro population of 45,000 in 1965 and 78,764 in 2011 is noted in footnote 46 on PDF p. 11).

study_design.comment: Note that the author's Spanish phrase 'revisión sistemática de material de archivo' refers to systematic archival historiography rather than a secondary epidemiological systematic review of literature.
study_design.value: Historical-institutional and environmental history single-case study based on archival records, municipal utility annual reports, corporate archives, parliamentary debates, hydrogeological reports, and legislation
